answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is genuine Thoreau, from the “Conclusion” of Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854). In full it reads: “I learned this, at least, by my experiment; that if one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams … he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours.” The wording here is the accurate original — not the popular paraphrase “Go confidently in the direction of your dreams.”

source.excerpt: I learned this, at least, by my experiment; that if one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams, and endeavors to live the life which he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours. He will put some things behind, will pass an invisible boundary; new, universal, and more liberal laws will begin to establish themselves around and within him… In proportion as he simplifies his life, the laws of the universe will appear less complex.
trail: The Walden Woods Project’s mis-quotation page prints this exact sentence as the “correct original from Walden.”
The full text of the “Conclusion” chapter contains the sentence verbatim, opening “I learned this, at least, by my experiment.”
Walden was first published in 1854, placing it firmly in the public domain.
source.excerptNote: The full passage opens with “I learned this, at least, by my experiment” — the popular quote simply begins mid-sentence at “if one advances confidently.”
source.rightsNote: The line is from Walden, first published in 1854 — well before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff — so the text is in the public domain worldwide.

author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.heading: About Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau was an American essayist, poet and naturalist, a central figure of New England Transcendentalism. From 1845 to 1847 he lived in a small cabin he built beside Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts; the book Walden (1854) distilled that experiment into a meditation on simple living and self-reliance. He is also remembered for the essay Civil Disobedience (1849).

misattribution.heading: The wording people get wrong
misattribution.intro: This one isn’t misattributed — it really is Thoreau. What circulates online, though, is usually a shortened paraphrase, not his actual sentence.

items.who: “Go confidently in the direction of your dreams. Live the life you have imagined.”
items.why: This tidied-up two-sentence version is by far the most-shared form, but it is not what Thoreau wrote. The Walden Woods Project lists it as a mis-quotation and prints the true original alongside it.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording asked about here is the genuine original from the “Conclusion” of Walden — it merely begins mid-sentence, dropping Thoreau’s lead-in “I learned this, at least, by my experiment.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Thoreau places this line at the very start of his “Conclusion,” as the lesson he draws from two years of deliberate, simplified living at Walden Pond. It is the book’s summation: live according to your own imagined life, and the ordinary rules bend in your favor.

The sentence has since become one of the most quoted passages in American literature — and, ironically, one of the most rewritten, usually shrunk to the crisper “Go confidently…” slogan on posters and graduation cards.
